• Other names: Royal Whiptail Catfish, Royal Whiptail Farlowella, Twig Catfish, Whiptail Catfish, Stick Catfish, Helicopter Pleco
  • Nitrate: less than 40
  • Diet: omnivore
  • Temperament: peaceful
  • Lifespan: up to 10 years
  • Colour: brown or yellow with tiny black markings
  • Keeping: easy to medium; breeding: medium

Royal Farlowella is not a true representative of the whiptail catfish genus Farlowella, although the name suggests so. It belongs to the closely related genus Sturisoma, a genus of armored catfishes native to freshwater habitats in Central and South America.

It is widely distributed in the Pacific slope rivers of Panama, Colombia and Ecuador, and the Caribbean slope rivers of Colombia.

The binomial name stems from sturio (German) meaning sturgeon and soma (Greek) meaning body, whereas panamense refers to its country of origin, Panama. The name hints at its sturgeon-like elongated body.
Most live in fast-flowing rivers with well-oxygenated water, cool temperatures and solid substrates.

The recommended minimum tank size is 120 litres. Because of its size, the fish needs a spacious tank with sufficient filtration and good water circulation.

The depth of the tank should be at least 2 times as long as the fish itself. Tank length matters more so they can turn around easily.

Add them only to a well-established tank of sufficient size and water volume. The species is easier to maintain than most whiptails.

The fish needs highly oxygenated water since it comes from oxygen-rich waters, and it is sensitive to still, oxygen-poor water. Provide ample water flow and excellent filtration (a powerful filter). An additional pump or powerhead can supply more current.

Perform regular water changes to remove excess nitrate, clean the substrate from time to time, and remove uneaten food and decaying plant matter.

Avoid overstocking. Too many tankmates limit the catfish's movement, increase the bioload and significantly decrease dissolved oxygen.

Temperature: 22–26 °C. They do not tolerate very cool water.

pH: 6.5–7.5.

Hardness: 4–10 dGH; very hard water is not recommended.

Lighting

Some aquarists say they prefer brightly lit aquariums. As a nocturnal fish, Royal Farlowella is not demanding when it comes to lighting, and lighting should be adapted to the needs of the plants in the tank.

Good lighting is also useful since it promotes the growth of algae on driftwood and other surfaces for the fish to eat. Even though high lighting significantly increases algae growth, it is not recommended for beginners: without understanding how the balance works, a beginner risks having so many types of algae that it turns the tank into a disaster.

Substrate

It is best to use smooth sand or fine gravel, as the fish spend a lot of time there moving gently and scavenging for food.

Water flow and oxygen

The fish appreciates fast currents and high oxygen levels to thrive and reproduce with ease. Provide a high degree of aeration and adequate filtration to maintain good water quality.

Keep in mind that oxygen solubility decreases as temperature increases. If the fish breathe heavily and hang around under the water surface, this is a clear sign of oxygen deficiency.

Decor

The tank should be decorated with rockwork and driftwood to provide hiding places and something to hold onto. They also appreciate twiggy branches and bogwood to rest and graze on during the day.

The tank should be densely planted, as this makes it more natural-looking and helps the fish thrive, reducing its stress levels.

Royal Farlowella are active algae and biofilm grazers, which make up a large part of their natural diet. Many aquarists report that they eat green spot algae and hair algae.

For best growth, the diet should contain greens and protein at about 70/30%.

They accept a variety of foods:

  • algae wafers
  • sinking catfish pellets
  • crushed fish flakes
  • spirulina
  • krill
  • artemia
  • meatier foods like live or frozen bloodworms
  • green vegetables such as zucchini, spinach, cucumber, cabbage

Sinking pellets and spirulina are formulated for bottom-dwelling fish.

Some aquarists say they prefer wood to live on but do not need it in their diet. Most professional breeders still insist on driftwood in the tank: while feeding on algae and biofilm they also rasp the wood and obtain fibres (cellulose) that aid digestion.

  • They do not compete well with other fish.
  • They are long and stiff, so they have trouble weaving around objects. Food should be put in the open where they can easily reach it.

The Royal Farlowella is a docile bottom-dwelling species that rarely bothers its tankmates. It is best to keep it with mostly non-aggressive, midwater fish to prevent competition for food at the lower levels.

It spends most of its time on the tank floor, roaming and scavenging uneaten food. It is typically nocturnal but becomes active in the daytime once established in a planted tank with plenty of rocks, twigs and bogwood.

During spawning, adult males may show territoriality, but only with a little pushing and chasing.

They are not very active and tend to stay in one spot for hours. They are also shy. A small group (3 to 5 individuals) is recommended, with more females than males. Stocking ratio 1 male to 2 females.

It is peaceful and a good addition to most community tanks. It is social, not a schooling fish, not active and peaceful.

Plants: although over 70% of the diet is plant food, they do not harm aquatic plants unless very hungry; they may sometimes keep grazing on algae until the leaves are worn.

Tankmates

Fish: guppies, platies, Corydoras catfish, rasboras, bristlenose plecos, Queen Arabesque L260 pleco, neon tetras, swordtails, pygmy cories, Otocinclus catfish, panda garra, etc.

Shrimp: not predatory, they will not hunt adult dwarf shrimp, but baby shrimp small enough to fit in the mouth may be eaten, though this is not common. For serious shrimp breeding, no fish should be allowed in the tank.

Snails: compatible with any freshwater snails.

Crayfish and crabs: keep away from all crayfish and crabs.

Avoid nippy tankmates that may nibble the tail filaments, e.g. pufferfish, serpae tetras, lemon tetras, black widow tetras, tiger barbs, gouramis, betta, goldfish, paradise fish, tinfoil barbs. Also avoid boisterous fish and related whiptails to prevent aggression and competition for food.

Pronounced sexual dimorphism:

  1. Adult females are slightly larger and stouter than males.
  2. Males are slightly more colourful than females.
  3. In males the head is shorter and wider.
  4. Males have odontodes (bristles) on the cheeks 1 to 6 mm long.

The first dorsal fin of the male is quite long. Under unfavourable conditions in an aquarium, odontodes can degrade and disappear completely.

Royal Farlowella reach sexual maturity at about 1.5–2 years. It is relatively easy to breed in the home aquarium provided you have a mature pair, favourable water conditions (swift currents, high oxygen, optimal temperature) and a larger tank, as they are vertical spawners. Always keep driftwood in the tank.

They can be stimulated with a series of water changes using slightly cooler water (1–2 degrees), simulating the rainy season. After the male secures a spot, the female mates with him; mating can last from 30 minutes to a few hours. They prefer to spawn on the glass where a constant current hits it. One male can fertilise eggs from several females.

Depending on size and age, a female lays 30 up to 150 eggs in small clusters on flat surfaces, usually the glass. The male chases the female and other fish away and guards the eggs until they hatch after about a week, fanning them constantly to reduce the risk of fungus.

Hatching and rearing fry

It is recommended to move the eggs and rear the fry in a separate, small, well-aerated tank with similar water conditions and a depth of less than 15 cm. Carefully slide the eggs about to hatch off the glass with an old card. Males do not eat eggs, but there are reports that females can do so by accident. Remove any fungused eggs immediately.

Eggs are quite large, up to 3.5 mm in diameter, light in colour and darkening as they mature. Incubation is 5–7 days. After hatching, the fry barely swim and need no food for the first 2 days as they feed on the yolk sac. Use this time to prepare natural food, because once they start feeding you must feed and change water constantly; with a large bacterial load in the water they die quickly.

Fry feeding – week 1

Juveniles grow best on a high-protein diet of finely powdered food, e.g. Sera micron, Hikari First Bite, spirulina powder, powdered chlorella. Flake food, algae wafers and artemia can be added, but only as a powder (use a coffee grinder). Always keep at least a small piece of driftwood in the rearing tank, as the fry grow fast and their digestive system needs fibre (cellulose) from the beginning.

The first 2 weeks are the most important. Without necessary nutrition during this time, the fry start dying at 3–4 weeks old. Feed at least 2 times a day after the 3rd day after hatching (3 times recommended), and siphon off excess food before refeeding.

Week 2

The fry are still too small to eat pellets and wafers.

  • Take a glass or plastic plate.
  • Moisten it with water.
  • Sprinkle powdered food on it.
  • Let it dry for a few hours.
  • Put it in the rearing tank, where the fry can scrape it off.

Week 3

In three weeks the fry grow to 3–3.5 cm and can be given whole pellets. Do not forget boiled vegetables. Water changes must be done daily (ideally 2 times a day), as fry do not like swings in water parameters.

Algae tricks

Keeping the rearing tank under 24 hours of light in advance lets algae grow so the fry do not starve, but lots of algae consume lots of oxygen, which can be dangerous for the fry, so do not do this unless you know how to balance the tank.

Another way is to use rocks in a separate container:

  • Use a transparent container (large bottle, spare tank, etc.).
  • Fill it with water from water changes.
  • Add many small, clean, aquarium-safe rocks such as marble chips and ceramic filter media.
  • Leave it under the strongest lighting available, ideally 24/7.
  • Use any plant fertiliser.
  • An airstone also boosts algae growth.
  • Once the rocks turn green, place a few in the tank to feed the fry.
  • Return the rocks to the container when they are clean.
